newsitem.title: USA: IPO market still quiet, deals percolating for February.
newsitem.headline: IPO market still quiet, deals percolating for February.

text.p: Few companies are planning initial public offerings this week, but rest assured, investment bankers are busy behind the scenes drumming up demand for deals due in late January and early February.
"The calendar will start to fill up in the next three weeks with filings," said Sheldon Sandler, managing director of corporate finance at Ladenburg Thalmann.
"There's still a lot of backlog left (from last year) and with continued strength in stocks, you can certainly expect more companies will want to go public," he said.
The IPO market is at the tail-end of a holiday nap. Last week, only a few small deals went public and only about ten are slated for this week.
PhotoElectron Corp. and RDO Equipment Co. could be winners this week, although premiums are likely to be slim, according to IPO Aftermarket editor John Fitzgibbon.
PhotoElectron, based in Lexington, Mass., has developed a photon radiosurgery system.

Fargo, North Dakota-based RDO Equipment, which operates John Deere industrial stores and agricultural stores, has seen its revenues grow at an annual rate of 33 percent over the past five years from $71.2 million in 1992 to $223.6 million in 1996, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Analysts say the market should kick back into full swing by early February.
"There are probably about five or six roadshows slated for this week," said Vincent Slavin, who tracks IPOs for Cantor Fitzgerald. "They should really start pumping out the week of February 8th."
Sandler said one sector industry he was looking to in 1997 for initial public offering is automobile dealerships.
"This sector seems to be picking up speed as a consolidation play. The car side is a very exciting area because it's ... still very fragmented and could provide a stream of new companies," he said.

Overall, the IPO market continues to look good, he said: "IPO's are always going to follow generally the conditions of the stock market. Until all of the venture capitalists are flushed out, and they have a lot of money right now, there's going to be an endless supply of deals from these guys."
